title: Recognising pain and distress
blurb: Read behaviour as communication, use DisDAT and carers' knowledge to spot distress, and look for the cause before assuming 'it's just behaviour'.
question: Pete, 48, has a severe learning disability and no speech. For two days he has been hitting his jaw and refusing his usual porridge. Staff say he 'is being difficult'. How should the nurse recognise and respond to possible pain?

teach.body: Many people with a severe or profound learning disability cannot say 'it hurts'. They show pain and distress through changes in behaviour, sounds, posture, facial expression, eating, sleeping and activity. NICE NG11 says behaviour that challenges often indicates an unmet need, and that self-injury may indicate pain or distress. In plain English: when behaviour changes, ask 'what is this person telling me?' before deciding it is 'just behaviour'.

The Disability Distress Assessment Tool (DisDAT) records how a person looks and behaves when content and how they look and behave when distressed, across appearance (face, eyes, skin), vocal sounds, habits and mannerisms, and posture. It builds a personal baseline so changes can be recognised. It is not a scoring tool: it describes this person's own signs. It was developed by Northumberland Tyne and Wear NHS Trust and St Oswald's Hospice.
teach.cite: DisDAT (NTW NHS Trust and St Oswald's Hospice)

teach.caption: Every person's columns are different. Carers and family complete it with staff while the person is well.

steps.label: Ask those who know them
steps.sub: Is this new? When did it start?

head: Possible cause
Clues to look for
rows: Pulling or hitting ear, head banging
Distress after meals or lying flat
teach.caption: Constipation, dental and ear problems are classic causes missed in people who cannot report pain.

teach.body: Diagnostic overshadowing is attributing signs of illness to the learning disability or autism, for example 'that is just how he is', so the cause is missed. It features repeatedly in LeDeR reviews. The antidote is the baseline: carers and family know what is new. Treat a change in behaviour as a possible sign of pain or illness, assess physically, and act on carers' concerns. Annual health checks include a care plan for managing pain (NICE NG11 1.2.1).

teach.h: Overlap: pain, illness and mental health
teach.caption: NICE NG54 asks staff to consider a mental health problem when behaviour changes (1.6.1) and to remember that a physical condition may be causing or masking it (1.7.2).

teach.h: Scenario: Pete in his care home
teach.body: Pete, 48, has been hitting his jaw and refusing porridge for two days. The nurse compares this with his DisDAT: hitting his face and turning from food are listed as his distress signs. She asks staff what is new, checks his bowel chart and temperature, and looks in his mouth: a molar is swollen. She gives prescribed paracetamol, arranges an urgent dentist visit with adjustments, and records the change so night staff can monitor his distress cues.

teach.text: Do not wait for a self-reported pain score from someone who cannot give one, and do not read a new behaviour as 'attention-seeking' or 'challenging' before a physical cause has been looked for. A change from the person's own baseline is the alarm bell.

items: Behaviour is communication; behaviour that challenges often signals an unmet need (NG11).
DisDAT records a person's own content and distress cues; it is a baseline, not a score.
Ask carers and family what is new; they know the baseline.
Look for physical causes first: teeth, ears, bowels, reflux, injury.
Avoid diagnostic overshadowing; update the passport and DisDAT.

summary: You can now read changes in behaviour as possible pain or distress, use DisDAT and carers' knowledge to compare with the person's baseline, and search for physical causes before attributing behaviour to the learning disability.

A.q: A student nurse asks what the Disability Distress Assessment Tool (DisDAT) is designed to do. Which answer is most accurate?
options: Give a numerical pain score from 0 to 10 for each shift
Record a person's own signs of contentment and distress
Diagnose the physical cause of a person's distress
Measure the severity of a person's learning disability
A.why: DisDAT documents how the individual looks and behaves when content and when distressed, creating a baseline so new distress can be recognised. It is not a scoring tool.

whyNot.0: DisDAT is descriptive and individual, not a numerical score.
whyNot.2: It helps recognise distress; finding the cause needs clinical assessment.
whyNot.3: It does not measure learning disability.

A.q: Which statement best describes diagnostic overshadowing?
options: Missing a diagnosis because a carer was not present
Treating pain before a formal diagnosis is made
Giving a second diagnosis that conflicts with the first
Putting signs of illness down to the learning disability
A.why: Diagnostic overshadowing is attributing signs or symptoms of physical or mental ill health to the learning disability or autism, so the illness is missed.

whyNot.0: Absence of a carer can contribute but is not the definition.
whyNot.1: Treating pain is good practice and is not overshadowing.
whyNot.2: Conflicting diagnoses are a different problem.

A.q: According to NICE NG11, what does behaviour that challenges often indicate?
options: An unmet need
A lack of boundaries
A psychotic illness
A wish for attention
A.why: NG11 says everyone involved should understand that behaviour that challenges often indicates an unmet need, which may include pain.

whyNot.1: NG11 focuses on understanding needs, not on boundaries.
whyNot.2: Mental illness is one possible factor, not the usual meaning.
whyNot.3: Attention can be a function, but NG11's general point is unmet need.

B.q: Joy, 36, has a profound learning disability. Her DisDAT says she hums and taps when content and groans and bites her hand when distressed. Tonight she is groaning and biting her hand. What should the nurse do first?
options: Give her PRN medication for agitation as prescribed
Distract her with her favourite music until she settles
Record the behaviour on an ABC chart for the team
Assess her for a physical cause such as pain
B.why: Joy is showing her recorded distress cues. The first step is to look for the cause, such as pain, constipation or infection, and treat it.

whyNot.0: Sedating distress without finding the cause risks missing illness.
whyNot.1: Distraction may help comfort but does not address a possible physical cause.
whyNot.2: Recording helps later; assessing for pain comes first.

B.q: Kwame, 29, has a severe learning disability and has started pulling at his left ear and banging the left side of his head. What is the most likely explanation to investigate first?
options: Self-stimulation because he is bored
A learned behaviour to gain attention
Pain such as an ear infection
A side effect of his anti-seizure medicine
B.why: New ear pulling and one-sided head banging point towards ear pain. Investigate physical causes before behavioural explanations.

whyNot.0: Boredom is a less likely first explanation for a new, one-sided behaviour.
whyNot.1: Attributing a new behaviour to attention without assessment is overshadowing.
whyNot.3: Medicine effects are possible but do not explain one-sided ear pulling.

B.q: A nurse is completing a DisDAT for Ivy, 52, who has a severe learning disability. When is the best time to complete the 'content' section?
options: When Ivy is well and settled, with people who know her
When Ivy is first admitted to hospital with an illness
When Ivy is distressed so that both states are compared
When the GP completes Ivy's annual health check in clinic
B.why: The content baseline is best recorded when the person is well, with carers and family who know their usual signs, so that later changes stand out.

whyNot.1: During acute illness her usual content signs may not be visible.
whyNot.2: Distress signs are recorded separately; the content baseline needs her settled.
whyNot.3: DisDAT needs input from those who know her well, recorded while she is settled.

C.q: Pete, 48, has a severe learning disability. For two days he has been hitting his jaw and refusing porridge, which he usually loves. A support worker says 'he's been difficult all week'. His temperature and bowel chart are normal. What should the nurse do next?
options: Start an ABC chart to find the function of the behaviour
Examine his mouth and arrange an urgent dental review
Offer a softer alternative to porridge and review in a week
Discuss increasing his PRN medicine with the prescriber
C.why: Hitting the jaw and refusing food suggest dental pain. Examining the mouth and arranging a dental review looks for the cause; analgesia can be given meanwhile.

whyNot.0: A functional assessment may follow, but a likely physical cause must be checked first.
whyNot.2: Changing food without finding the cause leaves possible pain untreated.
whyNot.3: Medication for behaviour risks masking dental pain.

C.q: Lena, 44, has a learning disability and cerebral palsy. Over a month she has become withdrawn, sleeps poorly and has stopped joining activities. Her bowels and teeth have been checked and are normal. Which next step best follows NICE guidance?
options: Record that this is a phase and recheck in 3 months
Consider a mental health problem and arrange assessment
Increase her activities to keep her more engaged
Start a sleep medicine to help her settle at night
C.why: NICE NG54 1.6.1 says staff should consider a mental health problem when behaviour changes, for example social withdrawal and loss of interest in usual activities. Likely physical causes have been checked (NG54 1.7.2 warns they can cause or mask the problem), so a mental health assessment is the next step.

whyNot.0: Dismissing a sustained change as a phase is a form of overshadowing.
whyNot.2: More activity does not address a possible mental health problem.
whyNot.3: NICE NG11 advises behavioural approaches before sleep medicine, and the cause is not yet known.

C.q: On a surgical ward, Rob, 61, who has a severe learning disability, lies still and grimaces after an operation. A nurse asks him to rate his pain from 0 to 10; he does not answer, so she records 'pain score 0'. What is the main problem with this record?
options: The pain score should have been taken by a doctor
Pain scores should be recorded every 4 hours after surgery
He cannot give a self-report, so his cues need assessing
The score should have been checked against his blood pressure
C.why: A missing self-report is not 'no pain'. His grimacing and stillness are distress cues; use his DisDAT or carers' knowledge and an observational approach, and treat.

whyNot.0: Nurses assess pain; the problem is the method, not who records it.
whyNot.1: Timing is not the main issue; the score itself is invalid.
whyNot.3: Vital signs can support assessment but do not replace observing his cues.

reteach.title: Spot the difference
reteach.question: If you know exactly how someone looks when they are happy, how would you notice they were in pain?

blocks.body: Pain recognition in someone without speech is a game of spot the difference. First you need the 'before' picture: how this person looks, sounds and moves when content. Then any change, such as a new noise, a new habit or a refusal, is a clue. DisDAT and the people who know the person give you that 'before' picture.

blocks.text: 'He's always like that' is a red flag phrase. Check it against the baseline with someone who really knows him.

explain.body: When someone cannot say they are in pain, changes in behaviour, sounds, eating or sleep may be their message. NG11: behaviour that challenges often indicates an unmet need.

test.q: A man with a profound learning disability starts biting his hand, which he has not done before. What is the most important first thought?
options: He wants staff attention
He may be in pain or unwell
He is bored with his routine
He needs a behaviour plan
test.why: A new self-injurious behaviour may indicate pain or distress and should prompt a search for a cause.

whyNot.2: Boredom is not the first explanation for new self-injury.
whyNot.3: A plan may follow, but a physical cause must be considered first.

explain.body: Records content and distress cues in appearance, sounds, habits and posture. A personal baseline, not a score.

test.q: Which feature of DisDAT is most important to understand?
options: It produces a pain score
It sets a national threshold
It describes the person's own cues
It is completed by a doctor
test.why: DisDAT describes this person's own signs of contentment and distress so changes can be recognised.

whyNot.0: It is not a scoring tool.
whyNot.1: There is no threshold; it is individual.
whyNot.3: It is completed with carers and family who know the person.

explain.body: Teeth, ears, bowels, reflux and injury are common hidden causes. Check them before deciding behaviour is the problem.

test.q: A woman who cannot speak becomes distressed after every meal and when lying flat. Which cause should be considered first?
options: Reflux
Dental decay
Ear infection
Boredom
test.why: Distress after meals and when lying flat points towards reflux.

whyNot.1: Dental pain is usually linked to chewing, not lying flat.
whyNot.2: Ear pain is not typically linked to meals and position.
whyNot.3: A pattern linked to meals and posture suggests a physical cause.

explain.body: Family and carers know what is normal for the person. Act on their concern; it is a key safeguard against overshadowing.

test.q: A mother says her son 'is not himself' but his observations are normal. What should the nurse do?
options: Reassure her that his observations are normal
Ask her what has changed and assess him further
Ask her to come back if he gets worse
Record her concern and review next shift
test.why: Carers recognise subtle changes. Exploring what has changed and assessing further avoids missing early illness.

whyNot.0: Normal observations do not exclude pain or early illness.
